summary: Defines a mobility option for Proxy Mobile IPv6 that carries information about the access network a mobile node is attached to. With it, the local mobility anchor can apply access-network- and operator-specific handling or policing to the node's traffic. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When your phone moves around, the main office wants to know which door you came through. This memo adds a note saying which network entrance you used.

subtitle: A Proxy Mobile IPv6 option that tells the anchor which access network, place and operator a mobile node is using.

tldr.problem: In a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain, the local mobility anchor may need to treat traffic differently depending on the access network a node is attached to, but the mandatory Access Technology Type option alone does not say enough.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile access gateway adds an optional Access Network Identifier mobility option, with sub-options for network name, geo-location and operator identity, to its Proxy Binding Update messages. The anchor stores the values and echoes them back in the acknowledgement.
tldr.outcome: The anchor can apply access-network- and operator-specific handling or policing. How it uses the data is out of scope, and the location data is sensitive and must be protected.

today: RFC 6757 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 7563.

sections.title: Why the Anchor Needs Access Network Details
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213) provides network-based mobility management. In some deployments, such as service provider Wi-Fi aggregation or a WLAN integrated with a mobile packet core, the local mobility anchor (LMA) needs to give differentiated service or policing based on the access network the mobile node is attached to. For example, treatment can differ between a network owned by the home operator and one owned by a roaming partner, or between different SSIDs on IEEE 802.11.

The Access Technology Type (ATT) option is already mandatory from the mobile access gateway (MAG) to the LMA, but it is not always enough. Learning the operator identity may not be possible without an extra out-of-band policy framework, which not every deployment has.

This document therefore defines an optional Access Network Identifier (ANI) option with sub-options so that the MAG can signal this information. The ATT option stays mandatory and must still be carried.
sections.eli5: The main office sometimes treats visitors differently depending on which entrance they used. This memo gives the entrance a way to say who it is.

sections.title: The ANI Option and Its Sub-Options
sections.content:
The ANI option is a mobility header option that can appear in both Proxy Binding Update (PBU) and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA) messages, at most once per message. It MUST contain at least one sub-option. Its Type is 52, its Length counts the octets after the Type and Length fields, and its alignment requirement is 4n.

Each sub-option has an 8-bit ANI Type, an 8-bit ANI Length and option data. Type 0 is reserved; types 1, 2 and 3 are defined below. Each of the three may appear at most once in an ANI option.

Network-Identifier (type 1)

Carries the name of the access network: the SSID for IEEE 802.11, the PLMN Identifier for 3GPP access, or the Access Network Identifier for 3GPP2. The ANI Length ranges from 5 to 32 octets. An E flag says the name is UTF-8 encoded, and implementations SHOULD use UTF-8. The Net-Name Length MUST NOT be zero. An optional Access-Point Name identifies the specific device, for example by its MAC address, and its length is zero if absent. For PLMN Identifiers, both MNC and MCC MUST be 3 digits, with a leading '0' added to a 2-digit MNC.

Geo-Location (type 2)

Carries the location of the network as known to the MAG, as an ellipsoid point in the WGS 1984 coordinate system. ANI Length MUST be 6. Latitude and longitude are each a 24-bit two's complement fixed-point number with 9 whole bits, with latitude from -90 to +90 and longitude from -180 to +180 degrees.

Operator-Identifier (type 3)

Starts with an 8-bit Op-ID Type, followed by up to 253 octets of identifier, which MUST NOT be empty. Type 1 is a Private Enterprise Number in network byte order, and type 2 is the operator's realm, a DNS-style name encoded as US-ASCII.
sections.eli5: The note has a label and up to three pieces: the name of the network, where it is on the map, and the company that runs it. Each piece can appear only once.

sections.title: How the MAG and LMA Behave
sections.content:
If the MAG is configured to support the option, it SHOULD include it, with the sub-options it is configured to carry, in every PBU it sends, including those for lifetime extension and deregistration. Each sub-option is included only when its configuration variable is 1, and only if the MAG can learn the value. If it cannot obtain a Network-Identifier or Geo-Location it MUST NOT include that sub-option, and it MUST NOT include the Operator-Identifier if it cannot learn the operator identity.

The values are typically configured statically per interface. They can also be learned dynamically, for example from DHCP Relay Agent Information (Option 82) or the DHCPv6 GeoLoc option, or through CAPWAP. The details are access-technology and deployment specific and out of scope. The MAG's Binding Update List entry MUST be extended to store the Network-Identifier, Operator-Identifier and Geo-Location.

The LMA extends its Binding Cache entry the same way. When a PBU carries the option, the LMA processes it and updates the entry; an LMA that does not understand it skips it. An LMA that understands the option and supports the sub-options MUST echo the accepted sub-options back in the PBA, unaltered. If a PBU has no ANI option, any stored access network information for that session MUST be removed. The LMA MAY use the data for access-operator-specific handling or policing of traffic, but how is outside the scope of the RFC.

If the MAG sent the option but receives a successful PBA without it, the MAG SHOULD log the event and, depending on local policy, MAY terminate the session, since this suggests the LMA does not understand the option.
sections.eli5: The entrance writes its details on every check-in note. The main office files them and writes them back to confirm. If the office sends back a reply without them, the entrance suspects the office cannot read the note.

sections.title: Configuration Variables
sections.content:
Three flags control whether each sub-option is used. They are EnableANISubOptNetworkIdentifier, EnableANISubOptGeoLocation and EnableANISubOptOperatorIdentifier. Each is available on both the MAG and the LMA, and each defaults to 0, meaning support for that sub-option is disabled.

When a flag is 1 on the MAG, the MAG SHOULD include the sub-option in PBUs; otherwise it SHOULD NOT. When a flag is 1 on the LMA, the LMA SHOULD enable support for that sub-option; otherwise it SHOULD ignore it. Both kinds of node MUST let system management set these variables, and the values MUST survive reboots and service restarts.
sections.eli5: There are three switches, one for each kind of detail, and all start switched off. A switch must stay where you put it, even after a restart.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
The option travels like any other mobility option, so it needs no special security of its own. The exception is the Geo-Location sub-option, which the RFC calls very sensitive. The PMIPv6 base specification already requires IPsec for signaling, and operators can use IPsec ESP with confidentiality and integrity to protect location data.

The introduction adds a privacy rule: the information is for use between infrastructure nodes and is not revealed to other mobile nodes or nodes outside the PMIPv6 domain. It MAY be exposed to specific outside parties only under an agreement approved by the subscriber, and otherwise MUST NOT be. If exposed outside the domain, it MUST be carried in a PIDF-LO that includes the subscriber's usage rules.

Because the MAG may learn values dynamically, for instance over DHCP, a lack of protection could let wrong access network parameters reach the LMA, causing wrong policy decisions. The suggested mitigation is to secure the path between the MAG and the access points, for example with IPsec or TLS.
sections.eli5: Where you are is private. The network keeps it between its own machines and shares it with others only if you agreed. It also locks the messages so nobody can slip in a fake address.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned mobility option type 52 for the Access Network Identifier option from the existing mobility option numbering space of RFC 6275. The document also creates two registries: the Access Network Information (ANI) Sub-Option Type Values, with types 0 to 3 as listed above, and the Operator-Identifier Type Registry, with types 0 (reserved), 1 (Private Enterprise Number) and 2 (realm of the operator). New values in both registries are approved through IANA Expert Review.
sections.eli5: The official number list now includes the new note type, 52, and two new lists for the kinds of detail it can hold.

items.label: Network-Identifier
items.desc: Network name such as an SSID or PLMN Identifier, with optional access-point name.

items.label: Geo-Location
items.desc: Latitude and longitude of the network as known to the MAG.

items.label: Operator-Identifier
items.desc: Identifies the operator, as a Private Enterprise Number or a realm.
